action.title: Initialize the GQA ragged attention world model

compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.hw_notes: H100 is well suited to BF16 tensor operations and high-throughput reductions, but ragged dimensions and small problem sizes can prevent good occupancy and utilization.
compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.notes: The operation contains substantial QK and probability-value dot products, but the effective matrix shapes vary per sequence.
compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.risk: Small or highly fragmented sequences may be launch- and scheduling-bound rather than compute-bound.

memory_bandwidth.notes: Q, K, and V are contiguous in head dimension, while sequence selection is indirect through prefix offsets. K and V can be reused across four query heads sharing one KV head.
memory_bandwidth.risk: Repeated K/V traffic and low reuse for short sequences can dominate before arithmetic throughput is reached.

register_pressure.notes: Stable attention requires running maxima, normalization state, and output accumulators for each query-head result; head dimension 128 makes output state substantial.
register_pressure.risk: Large query tiles or simultaneous head processing can reduce occupancy and increase spilling.

nodes.notes:
1) Problem classification: ragged, causal grouped-query attention with dense head-dimension dot products, softmax reductions, indirect sequence boundaries, and BF16 inputs/output plus FP32 accumulation and LSE. Fixed dimensions are 32 query heads, 8 KV heads, and head dimension 128; batch structure, query lengths, and KV lengths are runtime-dependent. 2) Canonical math: for sequence b, query position i, query head h, and KV position j below min(i+1+delta, Lkv), compute s(i,h,j)=sm_scale*sum_d q(i,h,d)*k(j,floor(h/4),d), normalize with stable log-sum-exp, then output(i,h,d)=sum_j softmax(s)*v(j,floor(h/4),d); LSE is log2(sum_j exp(s)). Query rows and heads are independent except for their per-row KV reduction. Online reduction and streaming over KV are valid. 3) Layout/access: q[total_q,32,128], k/v[total_kv,8,128] and output[total_q,32,128] are row-major with contiguous head dimension; indptr arrays provide indirect sequence slices; lse is contiguous over heads. Q is read once per assigned query tile, while K/V are reused across four query heads and potentially multiple query rows. Output and LSE are written once. 4) Regimes: tiny sequences or total work near one row are launch/latency-bound; medium sequences with many independent rows are occupancy and synchronization sensitive; long balanced sequences are compute/reduction-throughput-bound; strongly imbalanced ragged batches are load-balance and tail-efficiency-bound; very short KV relative to query can be bandwidth and fixed-overhead dominated. 5) Knobs: query/head mapping, sequence assignment, query and KV tile sizes, number of query heads processed together, KV reuse scope, register versus shared placement, staged memory movement, online versus materialized softmax, accumulation precision, causal-boundary handling, empty-sequence handling, and specialized short-sequence paths. 6) Skeleton: locate sequence boundaries, load a query tile, iterate valid KV tiles, form scaled QK scores, apply the per-query causal limit, update running max/sum/output state in FP32, then normalize and store BF16 output plus base-2 LSE; synchronization is only needed when data is shared across cooperating program instances. 7) Candidate families: query-centric fused attention favors independent output rows and low coordination for short or irregular sequences; sequence-tiled attention favors reuse across query rows for long sequences but raises state and synchronization costs; split-KV reduction attention targets very long KV ranges by distributing a reduction and combining partial states, but adds merge overhead and is unsuitable for small ranges. SELF_CHECK: the three children are mutually exclusive primary execution families for the first implementation experiment; their strengths depend on workload regime and they should not be combined as coequal top-level plans.

action.description: Implement an execution family that treats a sequence as the main unit of work and reuses its K/V data across multiple query rows while retaining one causal reduction per output.
action.rationale: Long sequences provide substantial opportunity to amortize K/V movement and exploit the fixed four-to-one query/KV head relationship.
action.title: Sequence-tiled attention

compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.hw_notes: The fixed head dimension and repeated query/KV head structure provide regular inner products, while sequence-level work can expose more sustained H100 utilization for large inputs.
compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.notes: The decomposition maps naturally to H100 tensor-core operations and has strong empirical support from the 13.24x speedup.

memory_bandwidth.notes: Sequence ownership provides useful K/V reuse across grouped query heads, but ragged tails and repeated tiles still expose bandwidth overhead.

register_pressure.notes: The mapping is viable on H100, though larger query tiles and four-head accumulation increase live state.

action.description: Implement an execution family that partitions exceptionally long KV reductions and combines partial stable softmax states into one output and one base-2 LSE per query-head result.
action.rationale: Splitting very long reductions can expose parallelism beyond one query result, but the added state merge and synchronization are only worthwhile in the long-range regime.
action.title: Split-KV reduction ownership

compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.hw_notes: Long KV ranges provide enough arithmetic to occupy H100 execution resources, and independent reduction partitions can expose additional parallelism.
compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.notes: H100 parallelism is unlikely to compensate for extra launches, global synchronization, and softmax-state reduction on these workload sizes.

memory_bandwidth.notes: Materializing or rereading partial softmax state adds traffic that is difficult to amortize across the observed short and medium ragged sequences.

register_pressure.notes: Each partial attention worker can have a manageable footprint, but partial-output state and a separate reduction introduce additional live data and resource-management complexity.

memory_bandwidth.notes: The length-7 tensor-core path has compact reads, but the unchanged generic length-35 path still reloads K/V across query tiles. These tiny cases are primarily under-occupancy and launch-latency limited rather than HBM-bandwidth limited.

register_pressure.notes: Length 35 still selects BLOCK_Q=16, BLOCK_M=64, eight warps, and a large FP32 output accumulator. That schedule can reduce occupancy for a workload too small to amortize its register footprint.

nodes.notes:
CURRENT:
- does: Batch-one lengths from 2 through 16, including the repeated 7-token case, use the fixed short-sequence tensor-core kernel. The 35-token case still uses the generic sequence-tiled kernel with BLOCK_Q=16, BLOCK_N=32, eight warps, and two stages.
- bottleneck: Launch latency and under-occupancy dominate length 7; compute scheduling and register pressure dominate length 35 more than memory bandwidth.
FOLLOW_THROUGH:
- aligned_with_intent: no
- if_no: The intended action was to specialize both repeated batch-one lengths 7 and 35. The implementation covers 7 only through the pre-existing broad <=16 path and leaves 35 on the generic schedule.
UPDATE_BELIEF:
- The solution passed correctness and remains very fast at 15.315x reference, but its 0.184394 ms latency is about 1.28% slower than the prior 0.182071 ms trace. This provides no evidence for the predicted improvement and confirms that the claimed length-35 specialization was not realized.
- next bet: Add an explicit, benchmark-guarded length-35 dispatch using fewer warps and test BLOCK_Q 8 versus 16 while leaving the successful length-7 path unchanged.

action.title: Length-35 low-warp schedule

compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.notes: BF16 tensor-core dot products and GQA reuse fit H100 well, but the current configuration is not specialized for the small length-35 workload and can pay excess scheduling and register costs.

memory_bandwidth.notes: The sequence-tiled path reuses each loaded query tile across KV blocks and reads K/V once per block; bandwidth is not the primary limiter for the short length-35 cases.

register_pressure.notes: The generic length-35 dispatch uses BLOCK_M=64 with eight warps, retaining substantial online-softmax and 128-wide accumulator state for a relatively small workload.

nodes.notes:
CURRENT:
- does: Uses sequence-tiled ragged causal GQA with online log2 softmax reduction, plus separate singleton and short-sequence kernels. For a maximum sequence length of 35, dispatch falls through the generic <=64 branch with BLOCK_Q=16, BLOCK_N=32, eight warps, and four stages.
- bottleneck: Latency and occupancy/register overhead dominate for the short length-35 workload more than memory bandwidth.

FOLLOW_THROUGH:
- aligned_with_intent: no
- if_no: The intended action was an explicit low-warp schedule specialized for length 35. The implemented dispatch instead uses the generic <=64 eight-warp configuration, so the measured solution does not directly realize the named low-warp tactic.

UPDATE_BELIEF:
- what changed after eval_result: The implementation passed and achieved 0.1841 ms versus 0.4970 ms for the reference, or 14.75x speedup, confirming that the sequence-tiled family and fused online reduction are highly effective. However, mean_vs_baseline_factor was unavailable, and the strong result cannot be attributed specifically to the intended low-warp length-35 schedule because that schedule is absent from the dispatch.
- next bet: Add an explicit length-35-range dispatch using the existing BLOCK_Q=8 low-warp configuration, then compare it against the generic eight-warp path. This should reduce launch-time and register overhead while preserving tensor-core reuse.

The expected 1.10x factor was relative to the unavailable baseline metric, so no direct PERF_GAP comparison is made; the 14.75x reference speedup is recorded separately.

kernel_summary: This is a ragged causal grouped-query attention kernel on H100: 32 query heads share 8 KV heads at a fixed head dimension of 128, with runtime-dependent sequence boundaries and total token counts. Each query-head output performs a causal reduction over its sequence-local KV range, requiring stable FP32 softmax accumulation, BF16 output conversion, and FP32 base-2 LSE. The main performance tension is between independent query-centric work that handles tiny and irregular cases well, sequence-level reuse that improves long balanced cases, and split reductions that may help only at exceptionally long KV ranges. Dominant risks are launch and tail overhead for small workloads, repeated K/V traffic for long workloads, synchronization and partial-state overhead for split reductions, and register pressure from 128-element output accumulators.
open_questions: What are the exact per-sequence query and KV length distributions in the omitted workloads, including the degree of imbalance and whether empty query or KV segments occur?
What is the baseline latency and throughput breakdown by workload, and which cases dominate the aggregate evaluation score?
Are q, k, and v guaranteed contiguous in the stated layouts at runtime, or must the kernel support arbitrary strides?
How strict is numerical comparison for BF16 output and FP32 base-2 LSE, particularly around causal boundaries and very large logits?
Does the evaluation include workloads where total_q and total_kv are large but each individual sequence is short, creating a high-launch-count regime?
What Triton and compiler features are available for H100, including tensor-core lowering behavior, warp-specialization support, and autotuning budget?
Are zero-length query or KV segments permitted independently, and what exact output and LSE behavior is expected for those segments?
Is the scalar sm_scale always finite and equal to 1/sqrt(128), or are materially different scales included?
